student_passage:
The Line of the Wheel

My father taught me to care for his old blue touring bicycle when I was young. He showed me how to patch tubes, oil chains, and adjust brakes. He was my first mechanic and the person whose patience I tried to imitate.[1] When he later gave me the bicycle, I kept a repair kit beneath the seat.

One Saturday, the chain began jumping whenever I pedaled uphill. My usual adjustments did nothing, so I wheeled the bicycle into a neighborhood repair cooperative. Along the co-ops tool wall[2] hung wrenches and unfamiliar gauges. I wanted to replace the chain, but a volunteer named Lena attacked[3] the problem more carefully.

She clamped the bicycle into a stand and asked me to turn the pedals. The rear wheel moved smoothly, but the chain wandered across the gears. Lena attached an alignment gauge near the derailleur. Lena and me[4] compared four readings around the rim. At that point in time,[5] I understood why adjusting the cable had never solved the problem: the metal hanger supporting the derailleur was slightly bent.

Lena demonstrated how to apply pressure gradually and measure after every small movement. Meanwhile,[6] I copied each reading onto a scrap of cardboard. The numbers drew closer together until the hanger stood more straighter than before.[7] When I turned the pedals again, the chain traveled quietly from one gear to the next. The repair had required less force than restraint.

[A] I kept the cardboard in my repair kit. [B] It reminded me that a symptom and its cause may be several adjustments apart. [C] A month later, I returned to the cooperative for its volunteer orientation. [D] The lesson had changed how I approached unfamiliar repairs.[8] Since that afternoon, I volunteered[9] at several open-shop sessions, often helping visitors slow down long enough to observe before replacing a part.

The blue bicycle still reminds me of the afternoons when my father taught me the basics. Now it also carries the memory of a crowded tool wall and a set of measurements made one careful turn at a time. Caring for it no longer means proving that I can solve every problem alone; it means knowing how patience and shared knowledge can keep a familiar wheel moving.[10]
